memory_candidates.content: bash `$PPID` inside a nested function-command-substitution (e.g. `snapshot=$(take_snapshot)` where take_snapshot() itself does `out=$(ps ...)`) names the intermediate subshell forked for the OUTER function substitution, not the true top-level script's own $$ -- because capturing a function's stdout via `$(...)` always forks a subshell (functions can't be exec'd directly), the process that ultimately execs an external command nested inside is a grandchild, not a direct child, of the real script. When a test harness needs to identify 'the real top-level pid' from inside a faked/mocked subprocess, walk the process's own ancestry with the real system `ps` and take the HIGHEST ancestor whose argv still matches the target script -- a subshell forked (not exec'd) retains identical argv to its parent, so the first matching ancestor found walking upward is not necessarily the real top-level pid; the last match before the first non-matching ancestor is.

For an orphan/leaked-process matcher (or any tool that can terminate processes), design exclusion as comm-identity allow-list + cgroup/uid ownership checks + a liveness check on a DIFFERENT process a candidate protects (e.g. a sleep-inhibitor's held target pid), never as an argv-substring match or an ancestor-only process-tree walk. An ancestor walk structurally cannot reach a sibling (e.g. the invoking session's own sleep inhibitor, a child of the same parent shell, not an ancestor of the invoker), and re-querying a PID captured in an earlier snapshot is a race if that PID is a transient subshell that has already exited by the time of the second query -- the fix must decide everything from ONE atomic snapshot, with the sole exception of the liveness check on a different, protected process. Deliberately trade recall for safety: a leaked process the allow-list fails to recognize survives (false negative), which is strictly preferable to ever terminating a live system daemon or another session's process (false positive).
